message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core is lightweight and shares resources. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Very simple instruction set, often SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – one instruction operates on many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Execution Model** | Serial or lightly parallel – each core can run a single thread at a time, but can switch between many threads quickly. | Massive parallelism – thousands of threads run concurrently, each doing the same operation on different data. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, complex memory management. | Smaller per‑core caches, relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory pools. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks, branching, I/O, small data sets, latency‑sensitive operations. | Data‑parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, convolution, image processing, physics simulations, deep‑learning inference/training. |
| **Power Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core, but overall power scales with number of cores. | Optimized for high throughput per watt; many cores share power budget. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded programming with standard languages (C/C++, Java, etc.). | Parallel programming frameworks (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, DirectCompute, Metal, etc.) or higher‑level APIs (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |

### Why the difference matters

- **Latency vs Throughput**: CPUs excel at low‑latency, single‑thread performance; GPUs excel at high throughput for many independent operations.
- **Branching**: CPUs handle branches efficiently; GPUs suffer when threads diverge because all threads in a warp/wavefront must execute the same instruction path.
- **Memory Access Patterns**: GPUs benefit from coalesced memory accesses; CPUs can handle irregular patterns better.

### Practical Takeaway

If you’re writing code that needs to process many similar operations on large data sets (e.g., image filtering, neural network inference), a GPU can give you orders‑of‑magnitude speedup. If your code involves complex decision trees, I/O, or requires low latency, a CPU is usually the right choice. In many modern systems, both are present and work together: the CPU orchestrates tasks while the GPU handles the heavy data‑parallel work.
